subject: Banking
title: The Great Depression and Bank Runs
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Great Depression and Bank Runs usable.

hook.text: Between 1930 and 1933, over 9,000 US banks failed. Families lost their entire savings overnight.

buildup.text: Banks had invested deposits in the stock market. When stocks crashed, banks couldn't return depositors' money.

discovery.text: Bank runs spread through fear. One bank closing made customers rush to withdraw from every other bank nearby.

twist.text: FDR declared a bank holiday in 1933, closing every bank for four days. He reopened only the ones that were solvent.

climax.text: 9,000 bank failures created the FDIC. Deposit insurance meant no saver would ever lose money in a bank run again.

punchline.text: 9,000 banks failed. America created deposit insurance so it never happens again.

quiz.question: What was created in response to Depression-era bank failures?

details.summary: Between 1930 and 1933, a wave of bank runs destroyed over 9,000 American banks, wiping out the savings of millions and deepening the Great Depression. The catastrophe led directly to the creation of the FDIC and modern deposit insurance.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Depression's bank runs remain the defining event in banking regulation. Every deposit insurance program, central bank emergency facility, and bank safety rule traces its origin to preventing a repeat of the 1930s devastation.
takeaways: Over 9,000 US banks failed between 1930 and 1933
Millions of Americans lost their entire life savings
The FDIC was created in 1933 to prevent future panic withdrawals

faq.question: Why did so many banks fail during the Depression?
faq.answer: Without deposit insurance, depositors who heard rumors about bank troubles rushed to withdraw, creating self-fulfilling prophecies. Even sound banks could not withstand mass withdrawals because they had lent out most deposits.

faq.question: How did the FDIC stop bank runs?
faq.answer: By guaranteeing that deposits would be repaid even if a bank failed, the FDIC eliminated the incentive to rush to withdraw. Since depositors knew their money was safe regardless, the panic that caused runs simply stopped.
